chapter_title: Chương 302: Hải Nội Net Phát Triển Nhanh Chóng

segments.title: Chương 302: Hải Nội Net Phát Triển Nhanh Chóng
segments.content:
Li Yanhong hadn't registered any social media accounts; his comments were made during a media interview.

And he was the one who initiated contact with the media!

Last year, the verbal dispute between Chen Guiliang and Li Yanhong became known nationwide. Now that Li Yanhong had suddenly come forward to dredge up the past, all eyes turned to Chen Guiliang.

The work phones of Chen Guiliang and his secretary were ringing off the hook with calls from reporters, and their work inboxes were flooded with related emails every day. Many newspaper reporters wanted to interview Chen Guiliang, hoping he would respond to the matter.

On Chen Guiliang's Xiaonei.com and Hainei.com personal accounts, many netizens also came to ask questions.

Chen Guiliang refused all interviews, only responding on his personal account:

"Baidu Tieba, Baidu Zhidao, Baidu Baike, Baidu Space, Baidu Soucang, Baidu Video… Baidu has so many Web 2.0 products. If a Web 2.0 bubble really appears, would Mr. Li be that happy? Or is it that you're hoping all your peers die off so you can dominate the market alone?"

"I also watched the video of O'Reilly's speech. The level of abstraction in his public speaking is on par with Mr. Li's. He thinks his roundabout way of speaking is very humorous, never saying things directly, always pausing for dramatic effect. As a result, he was quoted out of context by reporters who only reported half of his speech."

"It's true that Web 2.0 investment was overheated last year, just like real estate was the year before last, and heavy chemical industries were last year. Capital naturally flocks to where there's profit. You can't just say that because of overheated investment, China's real estate and heavy chemical industries are a bubble…"

"When real estate and heavy chemical investments overheat, the state intervenes to regulate them. But for overheated Web 2.0 investment, it can only be regulated by the market itself. So, it's natural for a batch of uncompetitive companies to die off. Those that survive will be battle-hardened veterans… In what field is this not the case? A thousand sails pass by the sunken ship; ten thousand trees spring forth ahead of the ailing one!"

"What that scoundrel O'Reilly really wanted to express was: Web 2.0 will give birth to great products, and the story of Web 2.0 is just beginning."

When reporters and netizens saw this, they suddenly realized that Baidu had the most Web 2.0 products of any internet company in China.

You could say Baidu was the largest Web 2.0-related company in China.

Bar none!

So, why was Li Yanhong jumping out again to be bearish on Web 2.0? Just to prove his own unique insight and successfully predict a bubble?

Or was it as Chen Guiliang said, that Baidu hoped its competitors would all die off, so it could dominate the field alone?

When reporters tried to contact him for an interview again, Li Yanhong started playing the disappearing act.

No response, no comment.

What happened?

It was simple. Baidu's executives and product managers all begged Li Yanhong to stop talking nonsense.

Although Baidu's Web 2.0 products didn't need to attract venture capital, this stuff was related to the stock price.

Right now, in the US media, questioning and being bearish on Web 2.0 had become the mainstream. Baidu had a ton of related products, and if Li Yanhong's remarks spread to the US, Baidu's stock price would surely plummet in response.

You're the boss of a publicly listed company, why are you bickering about winning or losing with Chen Guiliang, who hasn't even graduated from university?

Although Li Yanhong shut up, his comments had sparked the interest of the Chinese media in this year's Web 2.0 Expo.

Originally, the Chinese media's bearish trend-following on Web 2.0 wouldn't have appeared on a large scale until July. Because of Li Yanhong's remarks, the timeline was pushed forward by more than three months.

Newspapers and portal site channels related to IT and finance swarmed to report on what was happening in the US. Some media outlets also compiled a list of Chinese Web 2.0 websites that had died in the last two years, analyzing the fatal flaws of the Web 2.0 model.

Then, without Li Yanhong needing to say another word, the overall direction of public opinion completely shifted to being bearish.

Venture capital also became more cautious.

Last year, one could easily get investment. This year, it was impossible to get funding even if you prayed to all the gods.

Last year, two to three hundred video websites emerged in China. By April of this year, more than a hundred of them had gone bankrupt due to lack of funds.

Countless Web 2.0 entrepreneurs, especially those who couldn't get venture capital, wanted to strangle Li Yanhong with their own hands!

"Venture capitalists haven't completely lost confidence. 51 just completed its Series B financing of 15 million US dollars." Lü Zhihui had been closely following industry trends; he had to fly to the US next month to contact various investors in advance.

Chen Guiliang was at a loss for whether to laugh or cry: "51 is a real beast!"

All of Xiaonei.com's direct competitors had already died off, leaving only Qzone as an indirect competitor.

But Hainei.com had quite a few competitors, and 51's registered user count far exceeded Hainei.com's!

For the past six months, 51's registered users had increased by more than 5 million each month. It currently had a cumulative total of 72 million registered users, with over 20 million users logging in at least once a month!

Hainei.com's user growth over the past year had also been fierce. In September last year, it had just over 10 million, and by March this year, it had already broken the 20 million mark.

After seeing the data released by 51 following its Series B financing, Chen Guiliang called a meeting with the company's senior management, feeling very puzzled.

"What's this about 51 having 72 million registered users? Four months ago, the officially announced total number of internet users in China was only 137 million," Chen Guiliang said.

Xie Yang said, "As our biggest competitor, I've been keeping a close eye on 51. A large number of their users are internet cafe users who are not counted in the official statistics."

"51 initially attracted many users who were not very familiar with computers and the internet through malicious browser ads. This method was very effective, and we also followed suit, which contributed a good amount of data to Hainei.com's user surge."

"51 is also leveraging the 'pretty girl, handsome guy' effect. For example, when they only had a few million users, 30% of their users were from Shancheng. The reason for this is laughable; it was just because a very pretty girl from Shancheng used 51 and completed a video verification. Then, she attracted two million male netizens from Shancheng to register. It's just baffling."

"We also borrowed and adopted the video verification model. But Hainei.com's user base is different; many are unwilling to do video verification. 51's video verification rate is very high, focusing on authentic interaction. Many young boys and girls use this for online relationships, and there are also many perverts who specifically use it for hookups."

"Their 72 million registered users are heavily inflated; many are people who forgot their accounts and registered again. Why would they forget their accounts? Because there are too many internet cafe users who might go to an internet cafe once every half a month and are busy working the rest of the time."

"Out of their 72 million registered users, the peak concurrent online users is only 500,000. Whereas for our 23 million registered users, the peak concurrent online users is over 800,000. Our active user ratio is far higher than our competitor's!"

Chen Guiliang said, "You only talk about the good, not the bad. They have several million paying users."

Xie Yang explained, "Most of their so-called several million paying users are just 10 yuan a month VIPs. Moreover, 51 is playing word games. Their several million paying users aren't all paying every month; it's the cumulative number of users who have ever paid. A user might pay this month..."

"Actually, 51's user base has a higher overlap with Qzone's. It's mostly middle school students and young people who have just entered the workforce. They have their own circles and can have fun together. But our Hainei.com's user base is, on average, several years older."

The executive in charge of advertising was named Ma Yuqin, who had been promoted purely based on performance.

Ma Yuqin said, "Because of the different user bases, the advertisers on 51 are mostly online game and mobile phone companies. Especially games targeting internet cafe users, which perfectly overlap with 51's user base. It's very difficult for them to get other types of ads. But for our Hainei.com, the advertising content is much more diverse."

Despite 51's current great momentum, its user base was too singular, and its room for development was truly limited.

Later, it simply transitioned from a social networking site directly to a gaming community.

Even running a gaming community proved difficult, so it then transformed into a web game platform.

Finally, it became a "play-along" platform, featuring verified pretty female gamers and real-person matchmaking for games...

Its development path was quite bizarre.

It's hard to imagine that a web game platform and a "play-along" platform started out as an online social community benchmarked against Qzone.

Chen Guiliang asked, "Before the IPO roadshow, can Hainei.com's registered users reach 30 million?"
